detaileddescription.para: USBRadioPlus implements the RadioPlus Asterisk channel technology, native radio signaling, source processing, and the interactive tuning utility. This reference describes implementation contracts. The installed manual pages describe radio configuration and operation.

sect1.title: Source layout
sect1.para: Transmit observability uses opt-in Asterisk debug level 5 records prefixed URP_TXTRACE. Request, render, queue, write, and HID-call boundaries are distinct: generation or enqueue is not DAC playback, and HID return is not RF confirmation. OSS trace records report occupied bytes, including partial fragments. The PortAudio trace reports submission results rather than a per-write playback timestamp. Its playout guard separately uses the stream's output-latency estimate obtained at open. See the configuration manual for trace enablement and disable instructions. No new PTT policy or audio buffering is introduced by the trace.

listitem.para: chan_usbradioplus.c adapts OSS/libusb radio devices to Asterisk.
chan_usbradioplus_modern.c adapts the ASL radio-device API and PortAudio.
usbradioplus_channel_common.h defines shared channel lifecycle and tuning calls.
usbradioplus_channel_core.h defines PCM routing, the lock-free program ring, and echo state.
usbradioplus_native_tick.c directly renders local receive, final voice/telemetry processing, CTCSS/DCS, and DAC PCM in the native hardware callback.
usbradioplus_processing.h exposes validated profiles and live processing controls.
txagc_config describes the shared FFmpeg graph. Filtering, emphasis, equalization, dynamics, and limiting are implemented by that graph.
usbradioplus_radio.h contains carrier, CTCSS, DCS, measurement, and transmit-signaling state.
usbradioplus_ctcss.h, usbradioplus_dcs.h, and usbradioplus_hardware.h provide tone/code generation and parallel-port radio programming.
tests and tests_py contain executable unit, failure-injection, integration, configuration, utility, and install checks. Upstream reference fixtures are test data.

sect1.title: Audio buffers and units
sect1.para: The CM119 path runs at 48,000 samples per second with 960 samples in a 20 ms mono block. App_rpt starts at 8,000 samples per second; each channel stores its rate explicitly. The program-ring converter uses a nominal one-to-one ratio when its input and output rates are equal. Signed PCM spans -32768 through 32767. Native floating-point workspaces retain PCM amplitude units. FFmpeg format conversion supplies the graph's normalized audio representation. dBFS measurements use the full signed PCM range.

The app_rpt-to-hardware-callback program ring is the only cross-clock audio queue between app_rpt and the native path. It accepts PCM at the active app_rpt rate and renders from its first available sample; it has no source-audio startup fill or playback reserve. Its 110 ms occupancy target is a clock-recovery setpoint, not a fixed latency or keyed-transmit admission delay. One persistent libsamplerate stream converts the source rate to the native rate and gently adjusts its ratio for independent clock drift, including when the nominal ratio is one-to-one. This correction is independent of device and network jitter buffers and changes no PTT state. A temporary program-source shortfall is concealed smoothly by the callback renderer rather than rendered as an abrupt silence insertion.

Both adapters admit app_rpt program frames continuously, including idle silence. A native-parrot implementation may be the sole external program-audio producer only while it supplies native-rate samples through that same lock-free program ring. Legacy app_rpt echo is distinct and is not an external producer under this exception. PTT transitions preserve program-ring state. Native-rate input uses the same stream with a nominal one-to-one ratio. This continuous PCM flow affects audio only: program-ring occupancy neither requests nor releases PTT. The signaling engine retains ownership of the desired PTT state.

The hardware callback directly renders each prepared native block. It owns local receive processing, final voice/telemetry processing, CTCSS/DCS generation, and native DAC PCM rendering. The program ring is its only program-audio bridge: app_rpt normally produces it, and native-parrot playback may temporarily supply native-rate samples through it. No other audio worker is permitted; there is no per-channel native worker thread or native input/output worker queue. A program-source shortfall is concealed in the callback without changing PTT, COS, CTCSS, or DCS state.

The device writer submits one 48 kHz stereo block per completed capture interval, including while idle. COS and CTCSS decode do not control device write cadence. The OSS writer does not prepend silence when its queue empties. Its queue-depth bound and short/failed-write diagnostics still apply during idle operation. After a complete non-silent DAC submission, the adapter holds physical txPttOut through the measured or estimated device playout delay plus one native 20 ms block. It submits silence while draining, cancels the hold on a new key request, and never advances the hold for a short, failed, or underflowed submission. OSS measures queue delay after the write with an available-space fallback; PortAudio uses the output latency reported when the stream opens. This is a best-effort queue-drain guard, not a second PTT owner. PortAudio otherwise retains the ASL audio API's device recovery.

When the local chain is enabled, its enabled RNNoise and FFmpeg dynamics stages advance in the direct callback every native interval with receive cpu_saver_enabled=no. RX CPU saver bypasses those stages while the receiver is unqualified. Existing receive qualification, repeat routing, and final transmit muting still control audibility; processing continuity does not key the transmitter.

Hardware mixer settings use 0 through 999. Hardware gain is expressed in dB relative to setting 500. Receiver CTCSS decoder gain affects the detector input; it does not change voice gain. Native CTCSS is generated at the direct [ctcss] transmit_peak_dbfs PCM peak and mixed after transmitter dynamics and limiting. Hardware output gain then sets the DAC's analog level. Saturating PCM conversion prevents signed wraparound. The transmit preemphasis_enabled option controls only the composite graph's pre-emphasis stage. Final limiting uses the voice/telemetry profile's explicit lookahead-limiter controls independently of pre-emphasis.

Native DCS uses its own direct [dcs] peak_dbfs PCM peak and a fixed shared-FFmpeg spectral-shaping graph. It bypasses CTCSS generation, transmitter pre-emphasis, and speech processing, while sharing only the configured hardware output route and downstream hardware gain.

Each direction declares exactly one signaling method in its [receive] or [transmit] profile. Selecting receive CTCSS requires a non-disabled CTCSS source and a supported receive-tone list; selecting transmit CTCSS requires one supported default transmit tone. A receive-to-transmit map is required only when both directions select CTCSS; then both supported-tone lists must have equal length. Selecting DCS requires the corresponding DCS code in 000N- through 777I-style spelling (three octal digits followed by N or I). The configuration parser rejects an incomplete or invalid selected method before a channel can start, rather than allowing the radio engine to silently fall back to carrier behavior. For a configured profile, omitted clean-slate [receive], [transmit], [ctcss], and [dcs] options resolve to the concrete values in the shipped sample. Explicit scoped values take precedence over flat-section values. Integer signaling controls validate the exact storage units used by the channel adapter: receive squelch delay is 0511 ms, receive-on and transmit-off delay are 03000 20 ms frames, receive CTCSS relax is 0 or 1, and transmit/receive frequencies are nonnegative integral hertz. This keeps a successful reload from deferring a malformed numeric value to channel construction.

sect1.title: Thread and resource ownership
sect1.para: Profile snapshot getters clear their output when a radio profile is absent. Render paths must never consume uninitialized gain, routing, or CTCSS data while a profile is unavailable; the missing-profile status remains available to callers.

Each channel owns its native graphs, detector, program ring, and a callback-owned native renderer. Setup preallocates the renderer's resamplers, RNNoise state, echo recording, workspaces, and diagnostics. The hardware callback owns mutable per-frame renderer state, consumes the program ring, and directly produces the DAC block. It has no native worker to start or join and no native input/output queue to drain. The processing settings mutex protects profile snapshots. Never hold it while looking up or locking an Asterisk channel: app_rpt can read processing settings while holding channel locks. The scanner copies the needed profile data before channel lookup.

Native-parrot playback may be a separate producer only when it hands native-rate samples to the hardware callback through the lock-free program ring. Legacy app_rpt echo is not covered by this exception. No other audio worker is permitted.

The native radio callback, including carrier and CTCSS detector stages, uses only preallocated caller-owned state and prepared graphs. It must not call Asterisk logging, take locks, allocate memory, or perform file I/O. It directly executes the prepared FFmpeg graphs, RNNoise, and persistent sample-rate conversion when those stages apply; graph construction, reconfiguration, and destruction remain outside the callback. PTT is requested synchronously from the current signaling-engine state at the callback boundary. A completed non-silent DAC submission may hold physical txPttOut for the adapter's playout-delay guard while the callback feeds silence. Program-ring occupancy and audio shortfalls must never key or unkey the transmitter.

Native renderer measurements are published as coherent lock-free snapshots. Control-plane meters and reset requests must use that snapshot/request boundary instead of reading or changing callback-owned graph, RNNoise, SRC, or echo state directly. A reader receives the most recently published complete snapshot, or reports it unavailable after bounded retries rather than waiting for rendering; a pinned pair of snapshot buffers can therefore leave measurements briefly stale.

Configured radio traces remain preallocated in-memory diagnostic buffers. The obsolete receive/transmit capture toggles and file-capture path are absent, so they cannot add callback I/O or an alternate real-time path.

Each incoming-link audiohook owns a prepared FFmpeg graph, a preallocated conversion workspace, and a reader-pinned statistics snapshot through its Asterisk datastore. The callback synchronously processes the current eligible frame in place. It has no deferred link-rendering thread or input/output SPSC handoff queues. Graph preparation and replacement occur outside the callback; the callback uses an atomically published prepared graph and never rebuilds it.

A format or capacity mismatch, an unavailable graph, or a graph-processing error leaves the current Asterisk frame unchanged rather than allocating, reconfiguring, delaying, or replaying it. The prepared FFmpeg graph's bounded internal FIFO can report startup fill or runtime shortfall without creating a separate callback handoff. The published callback snapshot records those graph conditions, synchronous processing errors, and input/output levels. CLI readers pin a published snapshot buffer and can receive a briefly stale or unavailable snapshot rather than waiting for the callback. Link processing preserves the attached channel's negotiated sample rate and has no PTT policy.

Hook teardown detaches and destroys the audiohook, quiescing its synchronous callback before its graph slot or callback-owned workspace is released. A reload atomically publishes a complete prepared graph before changing link admission, so each callback uses either the old graph, the new graph, or a clean bypass. Hardware adapters own their device references and coordinate device and HID state when swapping USB assignments.

sect1.title: Building and checking the reference
sect1.para: Run make docs with Doxygen 1.9.8 or newer, Graphviz, and Python 3 installed. Generated HTML is written to build/doxygen/html; XML is written beside it. Doxygen checks undocumented symbols and enum values, parameter and return documentation, and invalid markup. Every diagnostic fails the target.

The pull-request quality workflow runs Doxygen concurrently with lint and static analysis. All three results must succeed before the Debian 13 amd64/arm64 test matrix. Ordinary pushes run only formatting, lint, and static analysis. Releases validate their artifacts from a main revision that has already passed the pull-request gate rather than rerunning it. Debian 12 packages are aspirational and may be built manually only when explicitly requested. Successful main-branch documentation publication rebuilds this reference for GitHub Pages.

Shell documentation uses double-hash comments. The documentation filter exposes actual shell function names and those comments to Doxygen without executing shell code or supplying missing documentation. Python uses standard docstrings with Doxygen commands for parameters and return values.
